--- FILE: CQ Morning Briefing/Recess update SCOTUS justices to testify before Congress.mp3 ---
Good morning. I'm Christina Karish and it's Wednesday, July 8th. This is CQ Roll Call's
morning briefing, and here are the top three headlines you need to start today.
Supreme Court Justices Amy Coney Barrett and Elena Kagan are scheduled to appear next week
before Senate and House Appropriators. It'll be the first time since 2019 that justices will face
lawmakers. The justices will testify before both chambers' financial service appropriation
subcommittees on July 14th to discuss the High Court's fiscal 2027 budget, but the justices
will likely face questions about the cases before them in recent years. This year's term featured
decisions that rebuffed President Trump's tariff regime and his attempt to redefine citizenship
through executive order, along with decisions that supercharged the ongoing redistricting wars
and gave presidents more power to fire federal officials. Next, the Senate could take up its
fiscal 2027 defense authorization bill as soon as next week, and equipment repair is among the areas
of debate among lawmakers. Senators Elizabeth Warren and Tim Sheehy have championed a so-called right
to repair provision in their chamber's bill. It would give the military services more control over
the data they need to maintain their systems more rapidly than they do today, and at a lower cost.
Civilian and uniformed leaders from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on down have supported
shifting control over data rights from industry to the government. The goal is to increase competition,
reduce prices, and ensure troops can fix their equipment on the battlefield.
And finally, sweeping moves to address sexual misconduct at the Capitol may not be coming
anytime soon, given the slow pace of change in Congress, but the Congressional Progressive
Staff Association said even, quote, low-hanging fruit could make a difference.
Staff safety is crucial, reads a Tuesday letter to lawmakers. The resignation of Representatives
Tony Gonzalez and Eric Swalwell amid misconduct allegations sparked calls for a broader reckoning
around culture on the Hill. Check cq.com for developing policy news. And for all of us in the CQ
Roll Call Newsroom, I'm Christina Karish. Thanks for listening.

--- FILE: Die Lage/Trump wendet sich von Selenskyj ab. Gewalt in Frankreich. Erleichterung bei Berlin-Sondierern..mp3 ---
Hier ist der Spiegel mit der Lage am Montagmorgen. Heute geht es um Donald Trump, der sich mal wieder von der Ukraine abwendet.
Wir befassen uns mit der Gewalt in Frankreich und wir blicken auf die Sondierer von Rot-Grün-Rot in Berlin.
Spiegel-Redakteurin Özlem Topshu hat diese Lage geschrieben. Am Mikrofon ist Philipp Nützig.
US-Präsident Donald Trump glaubt wenige Tage vor den Midterm-Wahlen offenbar, dank seines Diesel-Deals mit Russland die Preise an den heimischen Tankstellen drücken zu können.
Derweil müssen die Ukrainer massiven russischen Angriffen standhalten.
Kurz vor dem Winter bemüht sich Russland, möglichst viel zivile ukrainische Infrastruktur und Energieanlagen zu zerstören.
Die Abmachung über die Diesellieferung erfolgte unter Missachtung internationaler Sanktionen.
Außerdem, so Trump, solle die Ukraine, Zitat, verdammt nochmal, die Angriffe auf russische Raffinerien und Ölexporthäfen einstellen und sich einen neuen Präsidenten suchen.
Nur folgerichtig, dass Trump ein vom Kongress beschlossenes Sanktionspaket gegen Russland vorerst ausgesetzt hat.
Der US-Präsident lässt sich jetzt von jenen feiern, die diesen Krieg angefangen haben.
Moskau bezeichnete die Aussetzung der amerikanischen Strafmaßnahmen als, Zitat, historischen Moment.
Zumindest, das kann niemand bestreiten.
Noch vor wenigen Wochen sprachen wir über Schülerinnen und Schüler, die wegen schlechter Bedingungen an ihren maroden Schulen auf die Straße gingen.
Spätestens seit dem vergangenen Wochenende hat Frankreich es wohl mit einer landesweiten Protestwelle zu tun.
Überall im Land gingen Menschen auf die Straße.
Und nicht mehr nur die Jungen.
Nicht allein eine bestimmte politische Richtung, sondern eine breite Schicht von Menschen.
Nach offizieller Darstellung rund eine halbe Million, die unter anderem gegen die zu hohen Lebenshaltungskosten aufbegehren.
An vielen Orten schlug der Protest in Gewalt um.
Geschäfte wurden geplündert, Autos in Brand gesteckt, ebenso ein Rathaus, öffentliches Eigentum zerstört.
Auf einem Level, das sogar die hartgesottene französische Demonstrationsgesellschaft erschütterte.
Spiegelkorrespondent Leo Klimm berichtete aus Paris von in schwarz gekleideten vermummten jungen Menschen,
die die Polizei mit Gegenständen bewarfen.
Die französische Polizei wiederum ist nicht gerade dafür bekannt, Deeskalation auch als polizeiliche Aufgabe zu verstehen.
Ein halbes Jahr vor der Präsidentschaftswahl hat unser Nachbarland mit allerlei Krisen zu kämpfen.
Der Massenprotest, eine drohende Schuldenkrise, eine weiter auseinanderdriftende Gesellschaft.
Und wer ist schuld?
Richtig, die Einwanderung, zumindest nach Ansicht von US-Vizepräsident J.D. Vance.
Dabei ist die Krise 100% hausgemacht, wie Leo schreibt.
Es handele sich um ein, Zitat, französisches Versagen.
Die Vertreterinnen und Vertreter von Rot-Grün-Rot in Berlin haben am Wochenende Koalitionsgespräche beschlossen.
Den sondierenden Elif Ehralb von den Linken, Werner Graf von den Grünen und Steffen Krach von der SPD
war die Erleichterung anzusehen, dass es zunächst weitergeht.
Die Junge Union sprach von einem, Zitat, Kulturbruch.
Eine rot-grün-rote Landesregierung müsse von Informationen des Bundesverfassungsschutzes
und des Bundeskriminalamts ausgeschlossen werden, so die Forderung.
Es ist nicht völlig abwegig, als rechts der Mitte stehender Parteimensch
alles, was links oder weit links der Mitte steht, für absolut untragbar zu halten.
Und auch den real existierenden Antisemitismus muss man bekämpfen, egal wo man steht.
Das ist eine der offenen Flanken der Linken unter Wahlsiegerin Ehralb,
die ihren Laden in dieser Hinsicht in den Griff bekommen muss.
Was aber kein Freifahrtschein für den politischen Gegner sein kann,
Hysterie als Mittel der Politik einzuführen.
Wo ist denn dieses Maß und die Mitte, wenn man sie mal braucht?
Verliererin des Tages ist das Schamgefühl.
Am 9. Oktober versperrten jüdische Studierende
dem frischgebackenen stellvertretenden Landtagspräsidenten von Sachsen-Anhalt
und rechtsextremen Vordenker der AfD Hans-Thomas Tilschneider
den Zugang zur Synagoge in Halle.
Er wollte an der Trauerfeier zum Gedenken an das Attentat 2019 teilnehmen,
bei dem ein 27-Jähriger Jüdin und Juden ermorden wollte.
Es gelang dem Schützen glücklicherweise nicht, in die Synagoge einzudringen.
Er erschoss später allerdings zwei andere Menschen.
Die jüdischen Studierenden wollten offenbar einem Vertreter einer in Teilen rechtsextremen Partei
nicht auch noch dabei zusehen müssen, wie er Gedenken heuchelt.
Tilschneider hatte in der Vergangenheit den Anschlag relativiert.
Die Blockade hat nun ein Nachspiel, aber nicht für Tilschneider,
sondern für die Studierenden, wie der Berliner Tagesspiegel zuerst berichtete.
Die Polizei ermittelt wegen Beleidigung, weil sie Tilschneider, Zitat, Nazi genannt haben sollen.
Was heute sonst noch wichtig ist.
Die Bilder ähneln jenen aus Frankreich.
In Mailand haben erneut meist junge Randalierer Geschäfte geplündert und Autos angezündet.

AI debt gets a reality check. From American Public Media, this is Marketplace Tech. I'm

AI skills could be your ticket to a raise. But first, back to the jitters in the AI markets.
Stocks slumped this week on fears of rising borrowing costs. Already, Morgan Stanley data
showed debt issuance for AI-related projects slowed last month, down significantly from a record high
in June. The AI cloud computing provider CoreWeave, often pointed to as the face of risky AI financing,
it saw its bonds fall to levels typically associated with financial distress. And its stock price took
a hit, too. So could this be a sign of a larger trend? Here to discuss is Jewel Burke Solomon,
managing partner at Collab Capital.
It's saying to me that lenders are overall becoming a bit more cautious and asking some important key
questions to make sure that all of the debt issuance that happened over the past year, that the
infrastructure projects that companies are taking on actually can progress, actually can move past
permitting and power needs and all of these things to be able to be paid back. And, you know, you see
lenders just asking these harder questions and, again, slowing down a bit on the highs that we saw
back in June. We've seen a kind of a steady decline from that. But it's really about,
does the infrastructure, does the underlying business actually going to be able to support
all of this debt issuance?
Yeah, I think often when, you know, we've talked about the potential for an AI bubble bursting or,
you know, even just something like a, you know, a minor slowdown in the kind of AI build out,
often I think it's been predicated on, is the technology going to deliver? And I think,
you know, this moment kind of shows that, you know, there can be a sort of macro backdrop that
becomes more challenging, more challenging conditions on the ground for, you know, for
building data centers. All these things, aside from just like how good is the technology,
technology can affect, you know, kind of the future financial security of the industry and
maybe the whole economy.
Yeah, you're seeing the rubber meet the road in a real sense where companies are having to
grapple with permitting. If anyone's ever done construction projects, you know that they never
go according to plan. And so, you know, those are things that maybe the underlying underwriting
didn't factor in. And so now we're seeing that reality come to pass and kind of meet the moment.
So that's what companies are having to contend with. And lenders are seeing that and slowing down

Welcome to Seeking Alpha's Wall Street Brunch, our Sunday look-ahead to this week's market-moving
events, along with the weekend's top news and analysis. Hello, today is Sunday, October 18th,
and I'm your host, Kim Kahn. Earnings season continues to ramp up this week, so let's dive
in with three big names, SpaceX on Tuesday, followed by Tesla and Meta on Wednesday. Here's
some quick hits on what Seeking Alpha analysts have to say about those stocks from the bull and
bear camps. Capital Minded says SpaceX needs to win just 1% of the phone market against the big
three telecom companies, and its $1.66 billion off-rating profit would nearly cover its losses
for rockets and AI, with business and government revenue outpacing consumer growth. But Trapping
Value argues SpaceX could buy any of the three major telecoms at a 100% premium to their last closing
price, and it would still be a better decision than this CapEx war. For Tesla, Geneva Investor says the
gas price spike from the Hormuz crisis has replaced 30-45% of the old $7,500 EV credit in the U.S.,
acting as an even larger incentive. But Agar Capital argues that what's more incredible
than a flying roadster is that Tesla is valued at about $1.4 trillion, even as it continues to
struggle to convert revenue growth into profits and positive cash flow, sufficient to justify that
valuation. And Nelson Alves says Meta is transitioning from a cash-burning lab to a coordinated AI-driven
platform with multiple monetization paths. Meanwhile, Jonathan Weber says AI spending is still
having a negative impact on margins, and a better entry point is likely given how volatile shares
can be. Elsewhere on the earnings calendar, GE Aerospace, GM, Netflix, 3M, and United Airlines joined
SpaceX on Tuesday. Philip Morris, IBM, AT&T, Kinder Morgan, Lamb Research, and Texas Instruments weigh in
on Wednesday. P&G, Lockheed Martin, Honeywell, American Airlines, Comcast, and Western Digital are up
Thursday. Also this week, the Federal Reserve enters its blackout period ahead of the October 27th-28th
policy meeting. Monday also marks the 39th anniversary of the 1987 Black Monday crash.
In the news this weekend, Anthropic is circulating a draft AI safety bill among congressional lawmakers
that would establish federal oversight of advanced models while narrowly defining when officials could
seek to stop their release or use. According to Politico, the proposal would override certain
state requirements, giving the claw developer a direct role in shaping potential regulation of
its industry. In the proposal, government intervention to block a model would require
a foreseeable imminent risk of more than $1 billion in damage or death or serious injury to more than 50
people. And Elon Musk says drivers will be able to ask the roadster to perform any of the tricks the
company demonstrated autonomously, quote, as it will be sentient, unquote. We will have a wild looping
track, crazier even than Hot Wheels, at our Texas HQ where you can test out your roadster, he posted.
And for income investors, Colgate-Palmolive goes ex-dividend on Tuesday, paying out on November 13th.
Levi Strauss and Lowe's go ex-dividend on Wednesday, both pay out November 4th. And CVS Health goes ex-dividend
Thursday, with a November 2nd payout date. That's all for today's Wall Street Brunch. Look for links
to stories in the show notes section. Don't forget, these episodes will be up with transcriptions
at SeekingAlpha.com slash WSB. And join the elite community of real investors to unearth great

And one of the attack surfaces that I'm, like, the most concerned about is what they call the Internet of Things, right?
So these cheap devices that you buy and, you know, it might be a TV that streams a bunch of stuff or it could be, you know, a smart refrigerator or even not so cheap.

Your money briefing is still on a break, but we'll be back with more personal finance information for you in the future.
Until then, here's the news moving the markets this week.
Hey listeners, it's Saturday, October 17th.
I'm Imani Moise for The Wall Street Journal, and this is what's news in markets.
Our look at the biggest stock moves of the week and news that drove them.
Let's dive in.
The bull market turned four years old this week.
Happy birthday.
Very cute age.
But fears of higher interest rates crashed the party.
As of Monday, the S&P 500 had more than doubled since October 12th, 2022, marking the longest run for stocks since the rally that followed the 2008 crisis and ended in 2020.
Remember that pandemic thing?
But by Wednesday, investors weren't celebrating.
Inflation came in hotter than economists expected, adding to bets that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates again this month.
And those worries spilled over into the AI trade, where companies have been borrowing heavily to drive growth.
All those forces collided this week, leading the S&P 500 and Nasdaq to have their worst single-day performance since July.
Investors fleeing the stock market found refuge in bonds.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield notched its biggest weekly decline since February, as investors piled in.
The Nasdaq led the declines, falling about 4.5% for the week.
The S&P 500 lost just under 2%.
And the Dow bucked the trend, eking out a 0.7% gain.
CoreWeave has become a weather vane for one of the riskiest corners of the AI trade.
And this week, it weathered a tornado, making it our laggard of the week.
Shares plunged more than 25% this week, as investors grew increasingly nervous about the mountain of debt supporting the AI boom.
That's particularly bad news for CoreWeave.
The former crypto mining company now rents out powerful computer chips to AI developers.
But building that infrastructure is expensive, and CoreWeave has racked up at least $35 billion in debt to finance its growth.
And it's projected to burn through around $80 billion of cash over the next three and a half years, at least according to one analysis.
One of its biggest backers, NVIDIA, came to its defense Thursday.
CEO Jensen Huang said CoreWeave's strength was improving every day.
But Wall Street is getting more selective about which AI companies it's willing to finance.
The anxiety spread across the AI trade, with the most heavily indebted AI companies leading the sell-off.
Shares in rival infrastructure companies Nebius and IREN also tumbled, falling 25% and 23% respectively.
Our leader of the week is Apple, which finally joined the exclusive $5 trillion club.
Apple had flirted with a $5 trillion market value six times since July, but couldn't hold on to the milestone through the closing bell.
That changed Wednesday, when it became just the second company ever, after NVIDIA, to close above that threshold.
Overall, the iPhone maker's shares rose more than 2% this week, standing out against a broader tech sell-off to reach that record high.
One reason investors are excited about Apple right now?
Its new $2,000 foldable phone.
Pre-orders for the iPhone Duo opened Friday, and early demand appears strong.
Barron's is reporting that delivery dates for the Duo are already stretching into late January.
That's raising hopes that Apple's expensive new device could help revive sales,
particularly after signs that consumers weren't necessarily rushing to get their hands on new models.
Analysts noticed shorter wait times for the iPhone 18 Pro.
And finally, our number of the week is $188 billion.
That's how much investors owed Charles Schwab at the end of September, through what's called margin loans.
And those balances are nearly double the amount from a year ago.
Margin loans let investors borrow against stocks and other investments they already own,
boosting potential upside, but also magnifying potential losses.
The borrowing binge is being fueled by one strategy in particular.
It's called long-short tax-aware investing.
Here's how it works.
Investors borrow money to buy stocks they expect to rise and bet against stocks they expect to fall.
This creates opportunities to realize losses that offset taxable gains.
While the strategy can generate savings for clients,
its rapid growth creates risk for brokerages like Schwab,
which carry the loans on their balance sheets.
The surge prompted the company to, quote,
throttle growth by raising the minimum investment for some new accounts from $1 million to $10 million.
Rival Fidelity has stopped opening new accounts altogether.
But Schwab is already developing its own version of the strategy that's easier to manage,
because it doesn't see demand slowing.
As Schwab's CEO put it,
saving money on taxes is something clients love to do.

You can read about more stocks that moved on the week's news
